summary:
The Silent Explorers is a story game for children about NASA machines that were left behind in space.

Many NASA machines are still sitting on the Moon, on Mars and in deep space. Their missions are over, but their stories are not. In our game, these machines get to tell their own stories.

Players follow Aira, a girl from Miri, Sarawak, and ECHO, a small robot guide. Together they visit 16 real NASA machines. Players land Surveyor 1 on the Moon, drive the Lunar Rover, survive a dust storm on Mars with Spirit and Opportunity, dig for ice with Phoenix, and listen for marsquakes with InSight.

For each machine, kids hear its story, play a mini game, and learn real facts from NASA records. At the end there is a surprise: ECHO is a forgotten machine too.

Our game turns real NASA science into a fun adventure. It is made for classrooms, libraries and families in Sarawak and around the world, so children can learn that these machines are abandoned, but not forgotten.
details:
What exactly does it do?

The Silent Explorers is a story game for children. It is made for kids aged about 8 and above but everyone can play, but anyone can play it.

NASA has sent many machines into space. Some landed on the Moon. Some landed on Mars. Some flew far away into deep space. When their missions ended, most of them were left behind. They are still out there today, quiet and alone. Most people do not know they exist.

Our game gives these machines a voice. Each machine tells its own story: where it went, what it did, and what it found.

The story starts at Grandpa's house in Miri, Sarawak. A girl named Aira finds a dusty parcel at the door. The label says "ECHO-7, Return to Sender". Inside is ECHO, a small robot guide. ECHO takes Aira on a journey to meet the silent explorers.

Together they visit 16 real NASA machines. These include Surveyor 1, the Apollo Lunar Rover, the Eagle lunar module, Spirit and Opportunity, Phoenix and InSight, Ingenuity, Kepler and Dawn.

At the end of the game there is a surprise. ECHO is also a forgotten project, just like the machines. This helps children understand the meaning of our challenge: these machines are abandoned, but not forgotten.

How does it work?

Players start on a map with three places: the Moon, Mars and deep space. Each machine is a glowing dot. Four turquoise dots are the main story machines. The other dots are bonus machines.

When players tap a machine, they go through five steps.

  1. Discover: players brush away dust to find the machine. They see a real NASA photo or a NASA picture of it, and learn the basic facts.
  2. Story: the machine talks to Aira about its mission. Each machine has its own voice. A small tag shows what is a real NASA fact and what is the story voice.
  3. Play: players play a short game based on what the machine really did.
  4. Learn: players learn the machine's journey, how things were "then" and "now", and how its technology still helps us on Earth.
  5. Interview and quiz: players ask the machine questions. Then they check their answers with a quiz and the official NASA record.

Every game is based on a real mission event. Some examples:

  • Surveyor 1: land gently on the Moon. Players fire small engines and touch down slowly, like the real Surveyor did in 1966.
  • Apollo Lunar Rover: drive across the Moon and collect 6 rock samples, including the famous Genesis Rock. Then drive back to the lander before the battery runs out.
  • Spirit and Opportunity: drive Spirit with a stuck wheel, just like the real rover. Then drive Opportunity, and survive a giant Martian dust storm.
  • Phoenix and InSight: dig for ice with Phoenix's robot arm. Then listen for marsquakes with InSight.
  • Ingenuity: fly the little helicopter on Mars through glowing rings, then land softly.
  • Kepler: watch the light from a star and spot the small dip that shows a planet passing in front.
  • Echo 1 & 2(secret explorer): aim the radio dish in California at the shiny balloon and send a message when both stations can see it, so it bounces down to New Jersey.

What benefits does it have?

  • Kids learn by doing. They do not just read about a mission. They play it. Landing Surveyor slowly or driving Spirit with a stuck wheel helps them remember what really happened.
  • The facts are real. We checked the main dates, numbers and records against NASA sources. Each machine links to its NASA page, so teachers and kids can check for themselves.
  • It is clear what is true and what is story. The game marks real NASA facts and story voices with different tags. Kids learn to tell the difference.
  • It is easy to use. The game is one file that opens in any web browser. There is nothing to install and no account to make. Once it is open, it works without internet. This helps schools and libraries with slow internet.
  • It speaks to kids. The machines talk in friendly voices, and the words are simple. Music and sound effects keep kids interested.
  • It is close to home. The story is set in Miri, Sarawak. Malaysian children can see someone like them in a space adventure.

The game is for children, parents, teachers, libraries and space outreach groups.

What do we hope to achieve?

We want children to look up at the Moon and know that real machines are still there. We want them to know the names of these machines and the stories behind them.

We hope the game makes kids curious about space, science and engineering. We also want them to think about a bigger question: what happens to our machines after their job is done?

We hope teachers, libraries and outreach programs in Sarawak and around the world will use the game. It can start a lesson, a class talk or a family conversation about space.

In the future, we would like to add more machines, more languages such as Bahasa Malaysia, and a teacher guide with simple activities.

This is the story we wish we had heard when we were kids.

Tools, coding languages, hardware and software

We built the whole game as one web page.

  • GitHub
  • Vercel
  • Claude code
  • HDML

We did not need any special hardware or game engine. The game runs on a laptop, tablet or phone with a normal web browser.

NASA Data

Our game is built on NASA's resource list for this challenge. Every machine in the game is a real NASA machine from that list.

This is how we used NASA data:

  • Mission records: we used the NASA Space Science Data Coordinated Archive (NSSDCA) and NASA mission pages. From them we took each machine's launch date, landing date, end date, goals and discoveries.
  • NASA images: the Discover and Learn pages show real NASA photos and NASA artist pictures. One example is the Apollo 15 Lunar Rover photo AS15-86-11603. We also used NASA pictures of Spirit and Opportunity, Phoenix and InSight.
  • Real numbers in the games: the games use real mission numbers. Eagle touched down at only about 0.5 m/s. InSight's biggest marsquake was magnitude 4.7, on 4 May 2022. Ingenuity made its first flight on 19 April 2021.
  • Real science methods: the Kepler game shows how Kepler found planets by spotting tiny dips in a star's light.

We checked the main facts against NASA sources, and each machine in the game links back to its NASA page.

Use of Artificial Intelligence

Yes, we used AI as a helper.

  • We used Claude, an AI assistant made by Anthropic, to help write and fix the game code and video
  • We also Chatgpt and Gemini to help check facts against NASA sources.

Our team came up with the story idea, the characters and the design. We made the final choices and did the final checking.

We did not use AI to make any pictures. All photos in the game are from NASA. The machine voices come from the text-to-speech that is built into the web browser.

If you finish the main four mission finish the finale and the secert explorer can be unlock. For the certificate you must finish the main four and the bonus to unlock. You can refresh the game after finish play to play infinite time.

**NOTE: USE DESKTOP FOR BETTER EXPERIENCE**
